Weight shapes: input, weights, output of a conv layer
Convolution vs cross-correlation in deep learning
back: Libraries implement cross-correlation (no kernel flip). With learned kernels the difference is only a relabelling of the weights.
The same kernel weights are applied at every spatial position: far fewer parameters and translation equivariance.

front: Backward of a conv layer (matrix form)
back: $\bar W_{mat}=\bar Y_{mat}X_{col}^\top$, $\bar b=\sum\bar Y$, $\bar X_{col}=W_{mat}^\top\bar Y_{mat}$, then col2im (scatter-add, crop padding).

front: Why must col2im add instead of assign?
back: Windows overlap; a pixel used by several outputs receives the sum of their gradient contributions.
Route the upstream gradient to the arg-max position of each window; all other positions get 0. No parameters.

front: What did AlexNet, VGG, Inception, ResNet each contribute?
back: AlexNet: ReLU, dropout, depth on GPUs. VGG: stacks of 3x3 convs. Inception: parallel kernel sizes with 1x1 reductions. ResNet: residual blocks $y=x+F(x)$.

front: Why do residual connections ease training of deep nets?
back: $\partial y/\partial x=I+\partial F/\partial x$: the gradient has an identity path to earlier layers, and a block can learn $F\approx0$ (do nothing).
Same receptive field (5), fewer weights ($18C^2$ vs $25C^2$), an extra non-linearity.

front: A 1D conv of width k over word embeddings is...
back: A learnable k-gram detector (TextCNN): parallel and cheap, but blind beyond its window.
